Newborn Care

Home phototherapy for newborn jaundice: equipment, care and follow-up

Updated: October 5, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Phototherapy treats newborn jaundice with a medical light device that helps the body clear bilirubin. For some babies, an organized home service can provide treatment while the family stays together. Others need hospital monitoring or more intensive care. The decision belongs to the clinical team and depends on much more than how yellow the baby looks. This guide explains the practical questions to discuss before starting a home treatment plan.

Who can have treatment at home?

A clinician needs to assess the baby’s bilirubin result, age in hours, gestational age, feeding and overall health. A baby who is unwell, has risk factors for bilirubin-related injury or needs urgent intensive treatment may not be suitable for home care. Buying or hiring a lamp does not replace this assessment.

Eligibility differs between services. As one example, the American Academy of Pediatrics describes home LED treatment for selected babies who have already gone home: they must be at least 38 weeks’ gestation and 48 hours old, clinically well and feeding adequately, without previous phototherapy or known bilirubin-neurotoxicity risk factors. The bilirubin must be within a defined range around the treatment threshold, equipment must be available promptly, and daily blood testing must be possible. These are clinician-applied criteria, not a home eligibility test.

The practical arrangements matter too. Before agreeing to treatment, explain any difficulty with transport, language, understanding the equipment, electricity or overnight support. Needing hospital care does not mean that a parent has failed. The safest setting is the one that can deliver treatment and respond promptly if circumstances change.

Arrange a service, not just a lamp

Ask who supplies and checks the equipment, who teaches you to use it, where blood tests will happen and who contacts you with the results. Get a daytime and out-of-hours contact number, along with a clear route to hospital if treatment needs to change.

If equipment is loaned or rented, clarify collection and return, replacement for a faulty device, and any charges for delivery, consumables or monitoring. Costs and funding vary between places, so a price quoted in another country is not a useful guide to your total cost.

Do not book a fixed rental period on the assumption that every baby finishes within two or three days. Arrange how the loan can be extended or ended according to the clinical plan. Never continue unsuitable home treatment merely because equipment has already been paid for.

Understand the difference between the light source and the device

A light source describes what produces the treatment light; a device describes how that light reaches the baby. These are overlapping features, not separate generations that always become more powerful or safer.

Medical blue LED systems are widely used. Older equipment may use special fluorescent lamps, including compact arrangements, or other light sources. A household LED or fluorescent bulb is not equivalent to a medical phototherapy unit. Its colour or apparent brightness does not establish that it delivers effective treatment.

Fibre-optic equipment carries light to a pad through a cable. It does not necessarily use a halogen bulb: an LED light box can supply a fibre-optic pad. Likewise, a “blanket” describes the arrangement around the baby rather than proving that the device is weaker, stronger or free of precautions.

Ask the service to identify the exact model supplied. Its operating instructions and clinical suitability are more useful than labels such as “four-lamp,” “high-capacity” or “third generation.”

Overhead lights, pads and combined treatment

An overhead unit shines light onto exposed skin while the baby lies in the treatment area. Stand-mounted or tabletop designs can look different while using the same general approach. A covered or tunnel-shaped arrangement is another configuration; its shape alone does not establish how well it treats jaundice or whether eye protection is needed.

A light-emitting pad or blanket keeps the prescribed illuminated surface close to the baby’s skin. Some systems let a parent hold or feed the baby while treatment continues. The correct cover and contact matter: an ordinary blanket is not a substitute for the supplied pad cover.

A clinical team may combine an overhead source and a pad, or use another arrangement exposing more skin, when more intensive treatment is needed. Do not add lights or combine devices yourself.

The number of bulbs is not a reliable treatment dose. There is no universal rule that four lamps are safe but more must cause dehydration, or that a particular bilirubin number automatically requires a certain lamp count. The team selects a system that delivers appropriate light for the baby’s circumstances.

Set up the supplied equipment exactly as demonstrated

Before the first session, ask for a demonstration and then show the staff member that you can repeat the important steps. Identify the power control, light pad or lamp, cable connections, approved covers and any alarms. Know which parts you may clean and which parts must remain dry.

Use the stable, supported arrangement specified for the equipment. Keep ventilation openings clear, cables safely positioned and the treatment area away from accidental knocks. Ask the service about suitable room conditions rather than improvising extra heaters, fans or cooling.

For an overhead system, use the manufacturer’s specified distance and orientation. A universal instruction such as “25–30 centimetres away” cannot safely apply to every model. Moving a light closer can change both the exposure and the area treated; it is not a parent-controlled way to speed recovery.

Check the light and alarms as taught. If the device stops working, a cover is damaged or you cannot maintain the prescribed setup, contact the service immediately for a replacement or another treatment plan. A light that still turns on may nevertheless need maintenance, so leave output checks and lamp replacement schedules to the provider.

Protect the eyes and use the recommended clothing

Follow the instructions for the particular unit. Many arrangements require the baby to wear eye protection, and the mask must be positioned as demonstrated without covering the nose. Tell the team if it repeatedly slips or seems to interfere with breathing or comfort.

Do not assume that every fibre-optic blanket eliminates the need for an eye mask. For example, the manufacturer’s home guide for BiliSoft 2.0 instructs caregivers to protect the baby’s eyes during treatment. Another device may have different requirements; the instructions for one product cannot be transferred to another.

The team will explain how much skin should be exposed, whether the baby wears only a diaper, and whether wrapping around a pad is permitted. Unapproved layers can block the light. A diaper is used for hygiene; it should not be presented as proof that routine phototherapy damages the reproductive organs.

Positioning, sleep and comforting your baby

Keep the baby on their back unless a clinician has prescribed a different position for a specific medical reason. Do not routinely roll a sleeping newborn onto their stomach every two hours to illuminate another area. Ask how the device fits with the baby’s safe sleeping space.

You can still talk to your baby, reassure them and take part in their care. Ask which arrangements allow holding during treatment and when brief cuddling breaks are appropriate. Follow the equipment guidance rather than lifting or carrying an assembly that is not designed for it.

If the baby is unsettled, check the practical issues you have been taught to assess, such as a wet diaper, feeding needs or a displaced eye mask. Persistent or unusual distress needs clinical advice. Do not assume severe restlessness is simply frustration with the mask, and do not diagnose a rare light-sensitivity condition from crying alone.

Keep feeding effective

The baby needs enough milk during treatment. A sleepy baby who is not transferring milk well needs feeding support, not just more time under the light. Ask the team to watch a feed if you are unsure about attachment, swallowing or bottle-feeding technique.

Some light pads can remain in use during feeds. With other arrangements, the clinical plan may allow short interruptions for feeding, changing and cuddles. More intensive treatment can require uninterrupted light with a different feeding arrangement. Do not impose a universal schedule of taking the baby out every few hours.

Ask whether feeds, wet diapers and treatment interruptions should be recorded, and when the baby will be weighed. If additional milk is indicated, agree on the type and amount with the team. Breastfeeding can usually continue with appropriate support.

Do not give plain water, herbal drinks or home remedies to make jaundice clear faster. If the baby becomes difficult to wake or stops feeding, seek urgent help rather than waiting for the next planned feed.

Look after the skin and monitor temperature

Use only skin products approved by the treating team for the supplied device. Do not add oils, creams, improvised reflective materials or extra coverings in an attempt to increase treatment. Follow the cleaning instructions for the pad and its cover, and replace a wet or soiled cover as directed.

Ask how and when to measure the baby’s temperature and what to do with an abnormal reading. LED equipment may produce less unwanted heat than older designs, but that does not remove the need to check the baby and follow room and clothing guidance.

Phototherapy can be associated with changes such as loose stools or a skin rash. Report new or worsening changes, especially if feeding, alertness or urine output is affected. Burning, blistering or a distressed, unwell baby should never be accepted as the expected price of effective treatment.

A bronze or grey-brown skin change can occur in particular circumstances, including problems with bile flow. It needs clinical review rather than being treated as ordinary tanning. Pale, chalky stools or dark urine also require assessment.

Tell the team about conditions that affect light treatment

Certain rare conditions, including congenital porphyria, and medicines that make the skin unusually sensitive to light can change whether phototherapy is appropriate. Tell the team about known diagnoses, medicines and relevant family history before treatment starts.

A family history of skin cancer alone is not a standard blanket reason to prohibit all newborn phototherapy. Nor should every liver problem be treated as the same contraindication. The clinician needs to identify the cause and type of jaundice and decide what treatment is appropriate.

If the baby develops an unusual skin reaction or becomes unwell after treatment begins, contact the clinical team urgently. Do not attempt to distinguish a rare reaction from an equipment problem on your own.

Bilirubin tests show whether treatment is working

The team must follow measured bilirubin rather than appearance alone. Ask for the first repeat test time and how later results will be reviewed. A written home plan should identify who takes the sample and who decides whether treatment continues.

Testing schedules depend on the setting and guidance being used. The AAP home-treatment pathway requires daily serum bilirubin measurements. NICE’s general phototherapy guidance uses an earlier initial check and shorter intervals while treatment is being established. A timetable copied from an article should not replace your service’s plan.

If bilirubin is rising or not responding as expected, the team may need to check the equipment, reassess feeding, investigate another cause or admit the baby. Do not simply turn the device up, move it closer or wait for the rental period to end.

Keep a record of results and instructions. A missed test or delayed result is a reason to contact the service promptly; home treatment depends on reliable monitoring.

How long treatment lasts and what happens afterwards

Many courses are brief, but the necessary duration varies. The starting level, the baby’s age and risk factors, the cause of jaundice and the response to treatment all matter. There is no guaranteed 48- or 72-hour finish.

There is also no universal stopping target of “below 8 mg/dL.” The clinician uses the applicable treatment threshold and the baby’s progress. Do not stop because the skin looks less yellow or continue unnecessarily because a rental booking has time left.

Bilirubin can rise again after the light is stopped. Before finishing, confirm whether and when the baby needs another measurement, who will review it and how feeding and weight will be checked. The timing of this rebound follow-up is individualized.

Persistent jaundice needs the follow-up recommended for the baby’s age and circumstances. It should not be dismissed indefinitely as normal, but reaching day 14 alone does not mean that every otherwise well baby needs an emergency department. Pale stools, dark urine, poor feeding or illness make assessment more urgent.

Symptoms that need immediate help

Get emergency medical assessment if a jaundiced newborn is difficult to wake, is not feeding, becomes unusually floppy or stiff, has jerking movements or has trouble breathing. A temperature of 38°C or above, or 36°C or below, also needs immediate attention. Do not wait half an hour to see whether it settles.

No wet diapers, green vomit or another sudden serious change also needs urgent emergency assessment. Report fewer wet diapers, worsening jaundice or repeated vomiting promptly rather than assuming these are harmless treatment effects.

Follow the service’s escalation instructions and bring the latest bilirubin results and treatment details if you go to hospital. A baby who becomes unwell needs reassessment even if the machine appears to be functioning normally.

Light safety for the family and unsuitable substitutes

Use the unit only in the setting and manner described by its provider. Avoid staring directly into treatment lamps, keep other children from playing with the equipment, and ask about protecting another infant who may be nearby. Adult precautions are device-specific; a statement that every LED arrangement is completely risk-free is too broad.

Do not use a household fluorescent lamp, a decorative blue bulb or direct sunlight instead of prescribed phototherapy. They do not provide a controlled medical treatment plan. Apparent brightness cannot tell you whether enough useful treatment light reaches the baby.

If cost, access or an equipment problem makes home treatment difficult, tell the care team. The solution is another supervised arrangement, including hospital treatment when needed, rather than constructing a substitute at home.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

The American Academy of Pediatrics limits home phototherapy to appropriately selected babies with suitable equipment and dependable clinical monitoring. Its home-treatment pathway requires daily serum bilirubin measurement.

NICE emphasizes correct light delivery, safe positioning, feeding support and monitoring of temperature and hydration. Device instructions remain model-specific; a general article cannot set one lamp distance, eye-protection rule or stopping value for every system.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help caregivers organize feeding, diaper and growth observations to discuss with the baby’s care team. These records cannot measure bilirubin, choose a phototherapy setting or determine when treatment should stop.

When to seek help

Seek emergency assessment for a jaundiced baby who is difficult to wake, is not feeding, has breathing difficulty, is unusually floppy or stiff, has a temperature of 38°C or above or 36°C or below, or is producing no wet diapers. Do not wait for the next scheduled bilirubin check.

Evidence notes updated: October 5, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Home treatment requires clinical eligibility, suitable equipment and dependable bilirubin testing.
  • Light source, device shape and bulb count are different features; none alone determines suitability.
  • Follow the supplied model’s instructions for distance, covers, eye protection and handling.
  • Keep feeding and monitoring on schedule, and get help promptly if the baby becomes unwell.
  • The clinician decides when treatment ends and when follow-up testing is needed.

Frequently asked questions

Does a phototherapy blanket always mean no eye mask?

No. Requirements differ by device, and some pad systems specifically require eye protection. Follow the exact instructions supplied.

How many days should I rent the equipment for?

Arrange this with the treating service and allow for extension or early return. Bilirubin results and the clinical plan determine treatment length.

Should I buy a machine with more lamps?

Do not choose treatment intensity yourself. The clinical team needs to assess the whole device and the baby’s needs, not just count bulbs.

Can I stop when the yellow colour fades?

No. The decision requires measured bilirubin and a plan for any rebound check.

Can I hold or feed my baby while using the light?

Some pad systems allow this. Ask the service to demonstrate what is safe for your unit and whether treatment can continue during feeds.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
